questions.prompt: What does the Liskov Substitution Principle require of a subtype?

options.text: A subtype can replace its supertype only if it behaves the same way (behavioral subtyping)
A subtype must have fewer methods than its supertype
A subtype must never be instantiated
A subtype must depend on concrete classes

questions.explanation: LSP: a subtype can replace its supertype only if it behaves the same way — behavioral subtyping means it follows the same rules, not just the same method signatures.

questions.prompt: Why is 'Bird b = new Duck(); b.fly();' used as an LSP violation example?

options.text: Most familiar ducks cannot fly, so the substitution produces undefined behavior
Ducks are not birds
fly() is a private method
Birds cannot be referenced by variables

questions.explanation: Most familiar ducks cannot fly, so substituting a Duck where a flying Bird is expected gives undefined behavior — an LSP violation.

questions.prompt: What does the Interface Segregation Principle advise?

options.text: Clients should not be forced to depend on operations or interfaces they do not use
All clients should share one large interface
Interfaces should never be split
Clients should depend on concrete classes

questions.explanation: ISP: clients should not be forced to depend on operations/interfaces they do not use — make fine-grained, client-specific interfaces.

questions.prompt: In a statically typed language, leaving unused operations in a module can force useless recompilations and redeployments of dependents.
questions.explanation: ISP at the architectural level: remove useless operations from modules, otherwise they force useless redeployments and failures in unused features may cascade.

questions.prompt: According to the Dependency Inversion Principle, the most flexible systems have source code dependencies that refer only to...

options.text: Abstractions, not concretions
Concrete implementations
The main function
Database tables

questions.explanation: DIP: the most flexible systems are those whose source code dependencies refer only to abstractions, not concretions (as much as possible).

questions.prompt: Which practical rules does the DIP suggest?

options.text: Don't refer to volatile concrete classes
Don't override concrete functions
Never mention the name of anything concrete and volatile
Always depend on the most volatile implementation

questions.explanation: DIP rules: don't refer to (or from) volatile concrete classes, don't override concrete functions, and never mention the name of anything concrete and volatile.

questions.prompt: DIP violations can be entirely removed from any system in practice.
questions.explanation: DIP violations cannot be entirely removed — each system has at least one concrete component (e.g. main); violations should be minimized and kept separate.

questions.prompt: In dependency inversion, in which direction does the flow of control cross the separation line relative to source-code dependencies?

options.text: The opposite direction to the source-code dependencies
The same direction as the source-code dependencies
Control never crosses the line
It depends on the database

questions.explanation: All source-code dependencies point toward the abstract level, while the flow of control crosses the separation line in the opposite direction — the essence of 'dependency inversion'.
